result:
I like the hour after the rain stops, when the city is still wet but the sky has decided to stay.

The streets smell like hot asphalt and wet leaves, that specific mineral smell you can only get when water has been sitting long enough to cool everything down. People come out with their umbrellas half-closed, like they’re not sure if they’re done with them yet. Cars go by and throw up little halos of spray that catch the streetlights.

I was walking home with a paper bag of oranges. One of them rolled out when I hit a pothole and bounced, and a kid on a scooter stopped to pick it up for me. He didn’t say anything, just held it out and kept going. I think about that little transaction a lot. No thanks, no wave, just a brief, correct exchange between two people who will never meet again.

At home the kitchen window is still fogged from the shower I took earlier. I wipe a circle in it with my sleeve and look out at the fire escape across the way. Someone is up there in a towel, hanging laundry. It’s not even cold. They’re just hanging it anyway, because that’s what you do with clean things.

I put the oranges on the counter and peel one slowly. The skin comes off in one long piece, which feels like a small victory. I eat them standing up, juice running down my wrist, and I think about how many days I’ve done exactly this and how many days I haven’t noticed.

The radio is on low. Some old song I know the chorus to but not the verses to. My neighbor is practicing piano through the wall, badly, with a lot of determination. There’s a rhythm to a building when it’s settling in the evening: the hum of the fridge, the elevator dinging down, a dog barking three floors up and then being told to stop.

It’s not a dramatic hour. Nothing happens. And that’s why I keep coming back to it. Most of life is this quiet, ordinary, slightly damp in-between. You don’t write about it because it feels too small. But it’s the only thing that actually lasts.

I save the orange peel and put it in a glass of water on the windowsill. Tomorrow it will be bitter and brown and a little sad, and I’ll pour it out. For now it smells sweet.
